blocks.text: A **monitor** is an **output device** that shows text, pictures, graphics and video. It contains the screen and the electronics needed to run it. Another common name for a monitor is **VDU**.

blocks.title: Key terms
rows: Output device that displays text, images, graphics and video
**Visual Display Unit**, commonly used as another term for a monitor

blocks.title: Wrong full form
blocks.text: VDU stands for **Visual** Display Unit. 'Vast Display Unit' is incorrect and often appears as a wrong option.
This order is only a simplified exam sequence. It is a broad study guide, not an exact timeline of when each technology was invented.

Screen size is measured **diagonally** across the viewable screen, usually in **inches**. A 24-inch monitor has a nominal 24-inch diagonal. The measurement excludes the bezel (frame) and the stand. The diagonal is the distance between opposite corners of the viewable screen.

blocks.title: Diagonal of a rectangular screen
rows: diagonal = square root of (width² + height²), using the Pythagorean theorem
A screen 24 inches wide and 18 inches high has a diagonal of the square root of (576 + 324) = 30 inches

blocks.text: Size = **diagonal** (in inches). Resolution = **pixels**. Never mix these up: 1920 x 1080 is a pixel count, not a size in inches.
**Resolution** = horizontal pixels x vertical pixels. For example, 1920 x 1080 means 1920 pixels across and 1080 pixels down. Total pixels = width in pixels x height in pixels.

blocks.title: Exam accuracy
blocks.text: Full HD has 2,073,600 pixels; 4K UHD has **four times** as many (8,294,400). **2048 x 1080** is DCI 2K cinema resolution, **not** Full HD. Consumer 4K UHD is 3840 x 2160; cinema DCI 4K is a different format. VGA 640 x 480 is the commonly quoted legacy format, not a universal definition.

rows: Short for **picture element**: an individual element of a digital image
**Red, Green, Blue**; monitors combine light using this **additive** colour model
A conventional RGB pixel has red, green and blue subpixels; some panels use other layouts

blocks.title: Light adds up
blocks.text: Monitors make colour by **adding light** (RGB). Printers work differently: colour laser printers use CMYK toners.
If a pixel uses **b** total colour bits, the number of possible colour values is **2 to the power b**. More bits per pixel means more colours.

blocks.title: Per channel vs total
blocks.text: **8 bits per RGB channel** means 24 bits in total: 256 x 256 x 256, about **16.7 million** colours. But **8-bit total** means only **256** colours.

sections.title: Pixel Density, Refresh Rate & Response Time

rows: Pixels packed into each inch of screen
How many times the image updates every second (60 Hz = 60 refreshes per second)
Time taken for a pixel transition

items: At the same screen size, a higher native resolution gives a higher PPI and potentially sharper detail.
A higher refresh rate looks smoother.
Source quality and display settings still affect the final detail.

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.text: PPI = density, Hz = refresh, ms = response, nits = luminance. **Refresh rate and response time are different measurements.**

blocks.title: Nits
rows: Unit of **luminance**: 1 nit = 1 candela per square metre (cd/m²)
A higher measured nit value means greater luminance, commonly called screen brightness
About 200-300 nits for many basic office monitors; models vary and this is not a universal standard

blocks.title: Nits are not 'night visibility'
blocks.text: 'Night visibility brightness' is **not** what nits stands for. Nits is a unit name for luminance. Precisely, luminous intensity uses the candela, while luminance uses cd/m².

blocks.title: Core display types
rows: **Cathode Ray Tube**: electron guns direct electron beams onto a phosphor-coated screen. Bulky, deep and usually heavy; the oldest technology among those listed. Not a flat-panel display.
**Liquid Crystal Display**: liquid crystals control the passage of light; they do not make their own light.
A conventional 'LED monitor' is an **LCD panel lit by LED backlights**. The LED describes the light source, not a separate display principle.
**Thin-Film Transistor** LCD: an **active-matrix** display where transistors control pixels or subpixels precisely.

blocks.title: Backlights
rows: **Cold Cathode Fluorescent Lamp**: the backlight in older LCD monitors
Uses LEDs instead of CCFL; it can use less electricity than CCFL backlighting

items: CRT has no fixed addressable pixel matrix like an LCD, but saying it has 'no pixels at all' is an oversimplification.
LCD does not always mean CCFL: LED backlighting is also widely used.
A TFT LCD may use CCFL or LED backlighting, so TFT control and LED backlighting can exist in the same monitor.

blocks.title: LED is not a separate panel
blocks.text: An LED monitor is still an LCD. Liquid crystals form the picture; LEDs only provide the backlight. The old CCFL lamp is the fluorescent backlight that LEDs replaced.

rows: Small gas-filled cells are electrically excited into plasma (ionised gas); ultraviolet radiation excites phosphors to give visible light. A flat-panel technology.
Organic light-emitting elements produce light directly; individual pixels can switch off, giving deep blacks and high contrast. Very fast pixel transitions and wide viewing angles.
A conventional QLED is an **LED-backlit LCD** enhanced with quantum dots, which improve colour reproduction.
Microscopic inorganic LEDs emit their own light; distinct from Mini-LED.
Uses smaller LEDs in an LCD backlight, often giving more local-dimming zones and finer brightness control; can improve contrast. LCD pixels remain non-self-emissive.

blocks.title: One-word memory aids
blocks.text: **Organic** = OLED. **Quantum dots** = QLED. **Inorganic emitters** = MicroLED. **Tiny backlight** = Mini-LED. **Gas** = Plasma. **Electron gun** = CRT.

blocks.title: Exam traps
blocks.text: Self-emission is **not exclusive to OLED**: MicroLED and plasma also generate light directly. QLED = quantum dots, OLED = organic emitters. Electricity use depends on size, brightness, content and mode, so MicroLED is not universally the lowest-power or best choice. Saying OLED is 'always fastest' or 'always best' is too absolute.

blocks.title: Clue to answer
rows: Oldest type among the listed display technologies
Bulky, heavy, deep-bodied monitor; conventional non-flat-panel display
Organic self-emitting pixels; no separate backlight among the original choices
Very fast pixel transitions; wide viewing angles (expected exam answer)

blocks.text: LCD and LED are related; QLED and OLED differ. Mini-LED is a **backlight**; MicroLED is **self-emissive**. 'Most advanced' is subjective, not a fixed technical category. Least power consumption cannot be decided by the technology name alone; compare equal size, brightness, content and model specifications.

sections.title: Rapid Revision: Size, Resolution, Colour & Brightness

blocks.title: Facts to recall
rows: Measured diagonally, in inches; excludes bezel and stand

blocks.title: Technology truths
items: Conventional QLED is based on LCD technology.
OLED needs no backlight; CRT is not a conventional flat panel; plasma does not use liquid crystals.
Fluorescent lamps (CCFL) were used in older LCD monitors.
Higher native resolution at the same size raises pixel density (PPI) and can improve detail.

revision: A monitor is an output device; VDU = Visual Display Unit (never 'Vast').
Screen size is measured diagonally in inches, excluding the bezel and stand.
Resolution = horizontal pixels x vertical pixels; Full HD is 1920 x 1080 (not 2048 x 1080).
QHD is 2560 x 1440; 4K UHD is 3840 x 2160, which is four times the pixels of Full HD.
Pixel = picture element; RGB (Red, Green, Blue) is an additive colour model.
True Color is 24-bit RGB (about 16.7 million colours); High Color is 16-bit (65,536 colours); 8-bit total is 256.
PPI = pixel density, Hz = refresh rate, ms = response time, nits = luminance (cd/m²).
CRT uses electron guns and is bulky; it is the oldest display type listed and not a flat panel.
LCD uses liquid crystals, which do not emit light; an LED monitor is an LCD with LED backlights.
CCFL (Cold Cathode Fluorescent Lamp) backlit older LCD monitors; TFT is an active-matrix LCD.
Plasma uses ionised gas cells; OLED uses organic emitters; QLED uses quantum dots on an LCD.
MicroLED is self-emissive (inorganic LEDs); Mini-LED is only a small-LED backlight for LCD.
Self-emission is not exclusive to OLED: MicroLED and plasma also make their own light.
Simplified exam sequence: CRT, LCD, LED-backlit LCD, OLED (not an exact invention timeline).
